start: we become just by doing just acts
context: The heart of virtue ethics: we are not born good or bad; we become what we practise, the way a harpist becomes a harpist by playing.
prompt: What quality are you practising, whether you mean to or not?

start: to be happy takes a complete lifetime
context: Aristotle's happiness (eudaimonia) is not a mood but a whole life lived well. One good day doesn't make it, and one bad day doesn't break it.
prompt: What would a good life look like if you judged it by years, not days?

start: anybody can become angry
context: Anyone can feel anger or give money. Doing it to the right person, in the right measure, at the right time and in the right way is the real skill.
prompt: Where does a feeling of yours need better aim rather than suppression?

start: no one would choose to live without friends
context: Two of the ten books of the Ethics are about friendship. For Aristotle it is not a luxury of the good life but part of what makes it good.
prompt: Who would make your life poorer if they were gone?

parts: it is easy to fail and difficult to succeed
context: Virtue lies in a 'mean' between too much and too little, and there are many ways to miss it, but only one way to hit it.
prompt: Where are you erring on the side of too much, or too little?

start: The virtues therefore are engendered in us
context: We have a natural capacity for goodness, but it only becomes real through practice, the way a seed needs tending.
prompt: Which of your good capacities is waiting for practice?

start: Every art and every investigation
end: That at which all things aim.
context: The first sentence of the Ethics. Everything we do aims at some good, so the real question is: what is the highest good, the one we want for its own sake?
prompt: What are your daily actions ultimately aiming at?

start: It is therefore not of small moment
context: Habits formed early shape the person we become. The same is true of the habits we form now.
prompt: Which habit from your childhood still shapes you, for better or worse?

start: we are not investigating the nature of virtue
context: Aristotle reminds his students that ethics is not a theory to admire but a practice to live.
prompt: What do you know about being good that you are not yet doing?

start: he feels towards his friend in the same way as towards himself
context: One of Aristotle's most famous ideas: a true friend is 'another self', someone whose good we want as we want our own.
prompt: Who is another self to you?

start: The perfect form of friendship is that between the good
context: Aristotle distinguishes friendships of usefulness, of pleasure, and of goodness. Only the last lasts, because it loves the person, not what they provide.
prompt: Which of your friendships rest on usefulness, pleasure, or goodness?

start: The same exactness must not be expected
context: Ethics, says Aristotle, can't be as precise as mathematics. Wisdom includes knowing how much certainty a question allows.
prompt: Where are you demanding more certainty than the situation can give?

start: A man is temperate if he abstains from bodily pleasures
context: The test of a real virtue is pleasure in acting well. If doing the right thing still feels like a grim effort, the habit is not yet formed.
prompt: Which good habit has started to feel natural, and which still feels forced?

start: The beginning is admittedly more than half of the whole
end: more than half of the whole
context: Getting the starting point right shapes everything that follows.
prompt: What are you starting now, and is the starting point right?

start: it would seem to be obligatory, especially for a philosopher
context: Aristotle disagrees with his own teacher, Plato, here. Later summed up as 'Plato is dear, but truth is dearer'.
prompt: Which of your own ideas would you be willing to upset for the truth?

start: it is not easy to define in what manner and with whom
context: No rulebook can say exactly when anger is justified. That judgement has to be developed through experience.
prompt: When was your anger last right, and when was it not?

start: happiness above all else appears to be absolutely final
end: never as a means to something else
context: We want money, honour and even pleasure partly for what they bring. Happiness is the one thing we want simply for itself.
prompt: What do you chase as a means that you have started treating as an end?

start: rich men, rulers and potentates are thought especially to require friends
context: Wealth and power are worth little without friends to do good to, and are harder to keep without them.
prompt: What could you share today with someone you care about?

start: persons who wish another good for his own sake
end: must be known to its object.
context: Goodwill isn't enough for friendship; it has to be mutual, and both people have to know it.
prompt: Who might not know how much goodwill you feel toward them?

start: they seem actually to become better by putting their friendship into practice
context: Good friends make each other better, through time together and honest correction. Aristotle closes his books on friendship with this thought.
prompt: Who makes you better, and how?

start: Time seems to be a good inventor
end: anyone can fill in the gaps.
context: Aristotle sketches his ideas and leaves room for others to improve them. Understanding grows over time and through many hands.
prompt: What idea of yours could someone else help you improve?

start: man is by nature a social being
context: A good life is never lived entirely alone. For Aristotle, our nature is social.
prompt: Which relationships are part of your good life?

start: The man who runs away from everything in fear
context: Courage is the mean between cowardice and recklessness, and both extremes are formed by habit.
prompt: Are you leaning toward fear or toward recklessness lately?

start: the mere presence of friends is pleasant
context: Aristotle wonders whether friends really share our burdens, or whether their company simply makes the pain lighter. Either way, they help.
prompt: Whose presence could you offer to someone going through a hard time?

start: that which is best and most pleasant for each creature
end: this life will be the happiest.
context: Each creature flourishes by doing what is most its own. For humans, Aristotle thought, that means a life of thought and understanding.
prompt: What activity makes you feel most yourself?

start: it is held to be the mark of a prudent man
context: Practical wisdom (phronesis) is the skill of judging well about life as a whole, not just about one narrow goal.
prompt: What decision are you facing that calls for wisdom about life as a whole?

start: our definition accords with the description of the happy man
context: Happiness, for Aristotle, is active: something we do, not just something we feel.
prompt: What would living well and doing well mean for you this week?

start: he will not rejoice overmuch in prosperity
context: From the portrait of the 'great-souled' person, who is steady because they know what really matters.
prompt: What would it take to be steadier through ups and downs?

start: there is a state of mind in which a man may do these various acts
end: for the sake of the acts themselves.
context: Doing the right thing for the wrong reason isn't quite virtue. Goodness includes choosing the good for its own sake.
prompt: What good thing are you doing, and why are you really doing it?

start: Hence the importance, as Plato points out
context: Aristotle quotes his teacher Plato: a good education teaches us to enjoy the right things, not just to know them.
prompt: Which good things have you learned to enjoy?

start: pleasures and pains are the things with which moral virtue is concerned
context: Most of our failures come from chasing pleasure or avoiding discomfort. That's why virtue is mainly about training our likes and dislikes.
prompt: Which discomfort are you avoiding at the cost of doing right?

start: the pleasure perfects the activity, not as the fixed disposition does
context: For Aristotle, pleasure is not opposed to good activity; it is what completes it and makes it whole.
prompt: Which of your good activities also bring you pleasure?

start: although he will sometimes fear even terrors not beyond man
end: that is the end at which virtue aims.
context: The brave person isn't fearless. They feel fear and act well anyway, for the sake of what is right.
prompt: What are you afraid of that is still worth facing?
